source.title: Solving the Integrated Bin Allocation and Collection Routing Problem for Municipal Solid Waste: a Benders Decomposition Approach

accepted.question_text: For a garbage-accumulation-point municipal solid waste system, where residents deposit waste at shared garbage accumulation points and planners must jointly choose the locations and capacities of waste-bin combinations together with collection vehicle routes and schedules, can the Benders-decomposition-based mixed-integer programming approach for this integrated bin-allocation and collection-routing problem be tested on larger real-world instances than the Bahía Blanca instances evaluated so far, and what computational performance does it achieve on those larger instances?
accepted.context_brief: Scalability on larger real-world MSW instances

evidence.quote: When using GAPs, MSW management comprises the following design decisions: – The design of a pre-collection network, which consists in defining the location and capacity of GAPs. – The design and schedule of routes for collection vehicles.
We performed computational experiments using our approach on a set of real-world instances of two important neighbourhoods of the Argentinean city of Bahía Blanca.
Future work includes expanding computational experiments with larger real-world instances to test the scalability of the approach.

accepted.question_text: For the same integrated garbage-accumulation-point municipal solid waste planning problem in Bahía Blanca, what bin-allocation and collection-routing results are obtained when the computational experiments restrict the available bin combinations to bins that can be emptied by rear-loading trucks, rather than using side-loading-truck-compatible larger bins?

evidence.quote: Currently, in the door-to-door collection system, the company that performs waste collection in Bahía Blanca uses a fleet of rear-loading trucks. While only small bins can be emptied by a rear-loading truck, almost every bin can be emptied by a side-loading truck.

In this study we consider three bins that can be emptied by side-loading trucks to allow larger capacities at the GAPs and, thus, taking advantage of using economically convenient bin combinations (Section 3.1).
Further computational experimentation can be performed to include only bins that can be emptied by rear-loading trucks.

accepted.question_text: Can an allocation-first, routing-second method solve the integrated garbage-accumulation-point municipal solid waste problem effectively, where the first stage handles bin allocation and the second stage handles vehicle routing, given that this approach would make the master problem comparatively simpler than the routing subproblem and would require efficient vehicle-routing heuristics?

evidence.quote: Another research line is to consider an allocation-first routing-second method. In that case, the master problem would be comparatively simpler than the subproblem.
Such an approach would require efficient vehicle routing heuristics to work.

accepted.question_text: How can the integrated bin-allocation and collection-routing model for garbage-accumulation-point municipal solid waste systems be extended from a homogeneous fleet of collection vehicles to a heterogeneous fleet, including the small-capacity vans for spot operations already owned by Bahía Blanca?

evidence.quote: We consider an homogeneous fleet of vehicles.
We could also explore heterogeneous fleet of vehicles. Indeed, the city of Bahía Blanca already owns a fleet of vans of small capacity for spot operations.
